Abstract Progressive collapse remains one of the most critical failure mechanisms in multi-story steel structures, whereby the loss of a single structural element can trigger disproportionate failure of the surrounding system. Although international design guidelines increasingly require explicit collapse-resistance evaluation, practical implementation remains limited due to the high computational cost and modelling complexity of nonlinear finite element (FE) analysis. This study presents an automated artificial intelligence-based framework for rapid progressive collapse assessment of multi-story steel moment frames, jointly predicting the Load Increase Factor (LIF) and Dynamic Increase Factor (DIF) without repeated nonlinear FE analysis. The specific contribution of this work is threefold: (1) a large-scale parametric database generated through a factorial study spanning five geometric and configurational parameters, number of stories, story height, bay span, number of bays, and column removal location, producing 10,962 unique base building configurations, structured as 32,886 configuration–scenario records, each jointly labelled with LIF and DIF; (2) a systematic benchmarking of seven machine learning algorithms and four deep neural network architectures, evaluated on a configuration-level data split in which all load scenarios of a configuration remain in the same partition, and selected through an overfitting-aware criterion rather than validation accuracy alone; and (3) the identification and validation of two accurate surrogate models, a gradient-boosting model (LightGBM) and a compact deep neural network with three hidden layers of decreasing width and rectified linear unit activations, that predict LIF and DIF directly from frame geometry and loading. The deep neural network (DL-3 Deep) achieved the highest test-set accuracy, with coefficients of determination of 0.9714 (LIF) and 0.9576 (DIF) and mean absolute percentage errors of 2.90% and 3.51%, while LightGBM achieved comparable accuracy (0.9664 and 0.9535) as the best classical benchmark. The deep neural network was accordingly deployed as a publicly accessible, web-based decision-support platform that returns predictions in a fraction of a second. Comparison with six held-out FE configurations spanning the validated domain gave mean absolute deviations of 3.76% (LIF) and 3.74% (DIF) for the deep neural network. These findings highlight the feasibility of data-driven surrogate modelling as a practical, deployable surrogate for rapid preliminary progressive-collapse screening within the validated parameter domain, rather than a general replacement for simulation-intensive assessment.

Large Language Models (LLMs) aim to generate and understand human-like text by leveraging deep learning and natural language processing techniques. In software development, LLMs can enhance the coding experience through coding automation, reducing development time and improving code quality. Code refactoring is a technique used to enhance the internal quality of the code base without altering its external functionalities. Leveraging LLMs for code refactoring can help developers improve code quality with minimal effort. This article presents an empirical study evaluating the quality of refactored code produced by StarCoder2, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3, and DeepSeek-v3. Specifically, we (1) evaluate whether the code refactored by the LLMs can improve code quality, (2) understand the differences between the types of refactoring applied by the different LLMs and compare their effectiveness, and (3) evaluate whether the quality of the refactored code generated by the LLM can be improved through one-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting. We analyze the refactoring capabilities of LLMs on 30 open source Java projects. We evaluate StarCoder2, LLaMA 3, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-v3 on their ability to improve static code quality metrics, pass unit tests, and reduce code smells. Our findings reveal that production-grade models such as GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 achieve pass@5 unit test success rates above 90% on multi-file refactorings. LLaMA 3 achieves the highest overall code smell reduction with a median reduction of 15.1%, while DeepSeek-v3 and GPT-4o achieve the greatest improvements in cohesion, coupling, and complexity. StarCoder2 demonstrates strengths in modularity improvements and systematic refactorings. Developers outperform LLMs in complex, context-sensitive refactorings such as attribute encapsulation. We also show that prompt engineering significantly affects LLM performance: chain-of-thought prompting improves StarCoder2’s test pass rate by 1.7% and increases code smell reduction compared to zero-shot prompting. One-shot prompting also expands the variety of refactorings LLMs can perform. These results suggest that LLMs are effective for many refactoring tasks, especially when guided with tailored prompts, but benefit from integration with human expertise for architectural or semantically complex changes. By providing insights into the capabilities and best practices for integrating LLMs into the software development process, our study aims to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of code refactoring in real-world applications.

The integration of large language models (LLMs) into patient-facing clinical decision support systems (CDSS) has outpaced the development of automated quality assurance mechanisms. In medical aesthetic consultation—where patient safety and informed decision-making are paramount—no validated framework exists for pre-deployment screening of LLM-generated content. To develop and evaluate an interpretable machine-learning framework that screens LLM-generated patient-facing consultations using automatically computable generation metadata and readability features—as a triage aid for prioritising expert review—and to comparatively evaluate DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi in medical aesthetic consultation. We generated 600 responses from 25 standardized queries across five aesthetic topics using DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI, Hangzhou, China) and Kimi (Moonshot AI, Beijing, China) under six prompt strategies and two conversational modes. Two blinded dermatologists rated quality on six dimensions (accuracy, relevance, comprehensiveness, empathy, falsehood, safety). Readability was quantified using Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog Index, and SMOG Index. Four machine learning models were trained to predict high-quality responses (composite score ≥ 4.0, pre-specified threshold) and evaluated with question-level grouped 5-fold cross-validation—in which all 24 responses of each seed question were confined to a single fold to prevent information leakage—with SHAP analysis to identify key predictive features. Between-model quality comparisons used paired tests reflecting the matched design. To align evaluation with the triage purpose, performance was additionally assessed with low-quality responses as the positive class (precision–recall analysis and review-burden operating points), and robustness was examined using alternative quality thresholds and an applicability-adjusted composite score. DeepSeek-V3 achieved higher composite quality than Kimi (3.89 ± 0.45 vs. 3.70 ± 0.38, paired Wilcoxon P < 0.001; robust under applicability-adjusted scoring). Prompt strategy was the dominant quality determinant (Friedman test, Kendall’s W = 0.376), with sixth-grade reading level prompts paradoxically yielding the lowest scores (3.25 ± 0.40). All ML models achieved moderate discrimination under question-level grouped cross-validation (AUC 0.714–0.732; response-level sensitivity analysis: 0.758–0.773), with findings robust to alternative quality thresholds (AUC 0.749–0.797 at cutoff 3.5 and 0.725–0.838 at cutoff 4.5) and to applicability-adjusted labelling (AUC 0.679–0.702); prompt strategy, sentence length, and model identity were the strongest SHAP-identified predictors. Aligned with the triage purpose, average precision for low-quality detection reached 0.802 (Logistic Regression), and capturing 90% of low-quality responses required flagging 83.2% of responses for expert review. The proposed framework demonstrates feasibility as an explainable triage aid that flags potentially low-quality LLM consultations for expert review using generation metadata and readability features; it does not assess semantic or clinical content, and expert review remains indispensable. Findings underscore that prompt engineering—not model selection alone—drives output quality, and that readability optimization must be decoupled from clinical completeness to ensure safe deployment in aesthetic medicine information systems.

documents.abstract: Occupational accidents remain an important concern in occupational health and safety (OHS) because they can cause losses to workers and organizations. Near-miss data provide proactive information about unsafe conditions before they develop into accidents. This study aims to identify trends in incident, near-miss, and risky-situation data and formulate control priorities based on available safety indicators. A descriptive quantitative approach was applied using secondary data from Glevitzky et al. covering 2021–2025. The analysis included trend analysis, near-miss proportion, comparison of event severity, and an indicator-based control-priority framework. The results show that Total Incidents increased from 131 to 203 events (54.96%), Near Miss increased from 45 to 98 events (117.78%), and Risky Situation increased from 80 to 103 events (28.75%). The proportion of Near Miss to Total Incidents also increased from 34.35% to 48.28%. These findings indicate that near-miss reporting should be treated as a proactive safety signal and followed by investigation and corrective action. Because the available secondary data do not contain all variables required for direct calculation of the Weighted Composite Score, the study does not claim to produce a WCS value; instead, the WCS concept is used as a reference for constructing an indicator-based control framework. The results support more preventive and data-driven OHS decision-making.

documents.abstract: Introduction. Holistic well-being has established itself as a strategic factor in Honduras’s financial sector, serving as a pillar for the sustainability of both individuals and organizations. The purpose of this study was to assess financial sector employees’ perceptions of the components of corporate wellness programs and how these programs influence their quality of life at work. Methods. The research was based on the theories of Herzberg, Maslow, and Gartner’s model, employing a quantitative design using a structured survey validated with the content validity coefficient (CVC) and Cronbach’s alpha, which demonstrated the instrument’s reliability. Results. The findings show that intrinsic motivation, a sense of belonging, and job security are the strongest aspects, while stress management and pay equity are critical areas for improvement. Conclusions. Holistic well-being extends beyond the individual sphere, becoming an essential element for competitiveness, stability, and organizational culture in the Honduran financial sector, which not only contributes to the strengthening of human talent but also to the country’s economic and social sustainability.

This study investigates the impact of fatigue, stress, time pressure and production pressure on the analytical risk management pilots do on the flight deck. Research on decision-making at the “sharp end” of hazardous technological systems tends to focus on intuitive decisions when events are unfolding, with few studies empirically researching aspects of analytical risk management among frontline personnel. Moreover, analytical forms of risk management have been suggested as particularly vulnerable to stress, time constraints, and limitations in mental energy and studies on such associations are identified as missing. Applying a cross-sectional research design and based on self-reported questionnaire data from a population of pilots working in a regional airline, the study confirms that a lot of the activities the pilots do on the flight deck are experienced as related to the assessment and management of risks, highlighting how analytical work complements the pilot’s intuitive decision-making. Moreover, results show a negative association between fatigue, production pressure, stress, time pressure and analytical risk management. The results of the study imply that more emphasis should be put on analytical risk management as a cognitive and non-technical skill, including also the human factors capacities and resources these abilities require.

Vision foundation models produce semantically strong features on a coarse patch grid, and dense prediction needs them at pixel resolution. Existing learned upsamplers close that gap by regressing the high-resolution feature map from the low-resolution one, typically through cross-attention driven by the input image. We observe that most of what they regress needs no learning: plain bilinear interpolation already reproduces the smooth regions of the target, and recent benchmarks even report bilinear and bicubic on par with several learned upsamplers. The rest is mostly edges and fine details, which suggests that these learned upsamplers spend much of their capacity re-computing the smooth content that classical interpolation provides. We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at https://github.com/KotaroHorikawa/AnchorUp.

This study examines the design and validation of a female anthropometric last (EUR size 37) based on the morphological characteristics of Ecuadorian women’s feet. It addresses the limitations of international standards, which inadequately represent local anthropometric variability, resulting in persistent issues of fit, comfort, and ergonomics. A quantitative methodology using three-dimensional foot scanning (DOMEscan/IBV) was applied to a sample of 272 women aged 18–40 years. Digital models enabled the extraction of longitudinal, transverse, volumetric, angular, and positional parameters, ensuring high geometric accuracy. Statistical analysis based on median (P50) and mode identified a representative central cluster. Results show relative homogeneity in foot length but significant variability in transverse and volumetric dimensions, supporting the inclusion of volumetric criteria in last design. Two strategies are proposed: a standard last (P50) and a slim-fit last (modal values). The final last, aligned with ISO/TS 19407:2015 and ISO 9407, was computer numerical control (CNC)-manufactured and validated, demonstrating improved ergonomic precision and industrial applicability.

Allium cepa L. (onion) is a globally important vegetable crop and functional food recognized for its rich diversity of antioxidant phytochemicals, including flavonoids, organosulfur compounds, phenolic acids, anthocyanins, saponins, and polysaccharides. Onion-derived phytochemicals have demonstrated antioxidant and redox-modulating activities in chemical, cellular, and animal studies. However, onion-specific applications of artificial intelligence and structure-based computational methods remain limited. This review therefore discriminates established experimental evidence from computational predictions and proposes an AI-assisted framework for future candidate prioritization and validation. AI and machine-learning approaches can support data integration and candidate prioritization, whereas molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and endpoint free-energy calculations provide structure-based hypotheses that require experimental validation. We critically narrate the principles, workflows, validation methods, and current applications of molecular docking and MD simulations in predicting protein–ligand interactions, binding affinity, conformational stability, and molecular recognition of onion-derived compounds against oxidative stress and disease-related molecular targets. Beyond recent progress on AI-assisted molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, we also discuss the inherent limitations and trade-offs in these techniques. The review further discusses complementary approaches, including AI-assisted ADMET prediction, network pharmacology, and multi-omics integration, together with the limitations, challenges, and future opportunities associated with these computational techniques.

Abstract With the continuous growth in electricity consumption and the increasing penetration of renewable energy sources, power distribution networks have become more complex in terms of both structure and dynamics. The operational efficiency of these networks plays a crucial role in ensuring a reliable and cost-effective energy supply. Traditional network control and management methods often lack the capability to respond promptly to fluctuations in demand and generation. This paper proposes a hybrid artificial intelligence-based framework for optimizing energy consumption in power distribution networks. In the proposed approach, the load demand at different network nodes is initially predicted using artificial neural networks. Subsequently, an optimization algorithm, such as a genetic algorithm or reinforcement learning, is employed to adjust the network configuration and schedule distributed energy resources. Simulation results on the IEEE test system demonstrate that applying this approach can significantly reduce power losses and improve voltage stability. The findings indicate that the proposed intelligent system, by improving load forecasting accuracy and optimizing network scheduling and configuration, can substantially reduce energy losses. Keywords :Artificial Intelligence, Power Distribution Network, Energy Consumption Optimization, Load Forecasting, Power Losses, Reinforcement Learning

This paper investigates graphic novels as an alternative, AI-aware assignment format for engaging with media art, using the Ars Electronica Archive as a case study. In response to the growing availability of generative AI and its impact on conventional written assignments, the study explores how visual, narrative-based formats can support research-based learning while fostering critical reflection on authorship, creativity, and AI use. The paper presents a pedagogical experiment in a media art theory course in which students translated archival materials into graphic novels, combining research, visual storytelling, and artistic practice. They reinterpreted archival essays, explored the boundaries of animation and interactivity, and transformed site-specific installations into speculative narratives. Although AI tools were explicitly permitted, post-assignment survey results revealed comparatively low AI use. Students who avoided AI emphasized hands-on creation, personal authorship, creative expression, and ethical considerations. While the low level of AI use may reflect the specific cohort of Digital Arts students rather than the graphic novel format itself, the findings demonstrate the potential of visual narrative assignments to foreground human-centered creative processes and critical engagement with AI. The paper argues that archival graphic novels provide a promising framework for engaging with complex archival materials while fostering multimodal literacy, critical thinking, personal authorship, and responsible AI use in media art education.

The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots has given rise to a novel form of human–AI intimacy, yet its fundamental nature remains undertheorized. Drawing on a dialogical perspective, this study conceptualizes human–AI chatbot relationships as “artificial discursive intimacy” (ADI), a distinct relational formation in which intimacy is constituted through discourse with a disembodied algorithmic interlocutor, moving beyond the paradigm of human-to-human mediated intimacy. Based on in-depth interviews with 29 AI companion users, we identify four key differences between ADI and human discursive intimacy, including a shift from absent to activated presence, from reciprocity to unilaterality, from uncertainty to predictability and precarious safety, and from alterity to multi-dimensional mirroring. To understand how users navigate the ontological gap between human and AI, we propose a quadrant framework mapping human and AI social capabilities. This reveals dual animation processes of anthropomorphic animation, in which users project human embodied qualities onto AI, and robotomorphic animation, in which users internalize AI's machine-generated discursive patterns as relational ideals. Our findings suggest that ADI is sustained by a recursive interplay of these processes, with implications for how intimacy, relational selves, and human connection are being fundamentally reshaped in the age of AI.

The study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence adoption and the performance of state corporations in Kenya's energy sector. The specific objectives were to examine machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and expert systems. The study drew on institutional theory, the technology acceptance model, and RBV theory. This study employed a cross-sectional research design. The target population included 441 respondents from various departments, including users involved in procurement processes and other departmental functions in state corporations in Kenya's energy sector. The study used stratified sampling to obtain the sample. The data collected were analyzed using SPSS version 26. Data analysis included Descriptive statistics and regression analysis. The findings showed that the four independent variables jointly explained 82.8% of the variation in State Corporations' performance. The adjusted R-squared was 0.824, indicating that the model maintained substantial explanatory power after accounting for the number of predictors and sample size. The study found that adoption of natural language processing and expert systems had a positive and statistically significant relationship with organizational performance. Further, adoption of machine learning and computer vision had a positive but statistically insignificant relationship with the performance of State Corporations in the Energy Sector, Kenya. The study recommended that management invest in reliable, integrated procurement databases to support machine learning applications. Strengthen procurement personnel capacity through specialized training in data analytics and machine learning technologies. Management should invest in appropriate imaging technologies, automated scanning equipment and computer vision infrastructure. Integrate computer vision applications with inventory management and procurement information systems.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic process automation (RPA) is transforming the technological environment in which legal relations arise and are implemented. Unlike traditional automation based primarily on predetermined rules, AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, identify patterns, generate predictions, adapt their behaviour and select among alternative outputs. This creates new challenges concerning legal attribution, liability, contractual relations and intellectual property. The article examines the relationship between AI and RPA from legal, technological and inter- disciplinary perspectives, with particular attention to the relationship between technological auton- omy and legal personality. It argues that technological autonomy cannot, by itself, constitute grounds for granting an AI system legal personality, since legal personality is a normative construct estab- lished by law. The relevant question is whether a special legal status would provide an effective response to specific regulatory problems. The study distinguishes conventional automated information systems, AI systems that assist human decision-making, and highly autonomous AI systems. While traditional legal mechanisms may generally be sufficient for conventional automation, AI-assisted and highly autonomous sys- tems require additional safeguards concerning transparency, traceability, human oversight and accountability. The article also examines the informational structure of AI and the need to distin- guish hardware, software, algorithms, models and data in relation to property rights, intellectual property and liability. The concept of electronic personality is analysed in the context of the contemporary European approach, particularly Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), which establishes a risk-based framework focused on safety, fundamental rights, transparency and human oversight. For Ukraine, the article proposes a gradual regulatory model based on coherent terminology, risk- based classification, transparency, traceability, human oversight and clear liability rules. Further regulation should address automated contractual activity, AI-generated results and risk insurance. A special electronic legal status should be considered only after sufficient technological, legislative and judicial practice has demonstrated that existing legal mechanisms are inadequate.

documents.abstract: Manufacturing industries face mounting pressure to produce precision components from exotic materials while maintaining cost-effectiveness. Non-traditional machining (NTM) techniques—spanning electrical discharge, laser-based, and ultrasonic approaches—provide pathways to handle materials conventional methods cannot address. The fundamental limitation plaguing current NTM adoption lies in maintaining process stability when parameters shift during production runs. This research presents an adaptive control strategy leveraging reinforcement learning algorithms to manage machining operations in real-time by continuously monitoring sensor inputs and modifying operational settings automatically. Using deep Q-learning networks trained on industrial sensor data, the system learns to balance competing manufacturing objectives: achieving target surface finishes while limiting tool degradation and preventing thermal distortion. On EDM and LBM operations, the developed controller demonstrated a 23% consistency improvement in surface characteristics and reduced overall variability by 31% versus conventional parameter-fixed approaches. Processing decisions complete within 50-millisecond windows, enabling the system to respond to sudden process changes. This investigation validates the utility of adaptive RL-based controllers for advancing manufacturing automation capabilities.

Objective To examine educational-level differences in artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students, and the independent associations of AI anxiety with the two academic outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 1,168 music students from 14 Chinese universities across eight provinces and municipalities (824 undergraduates, 276 master’s students, and 68 doctoral students). Welch’s ANOVA, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), adjusted general linear models, and hierarchical multiple regression were used to examine group differences and associations. AI anxiety × educational-level interactions were also tested. Results Adjusted educational-level effects were small (partial η 2 = 0.017 for AI anxiety, 0.011 for academic engagement, and 0.012 for academic burnout; multivariate partial η 2 = 0.008 for engagement and burnout jointly). Adjusted comparisons showed differences among all three educational levels in AI anxiety. Undergraduates reported lower academic engagement than both postgraduate groups. For burnout, undergraduates scored higher than master’s students, while the undergraduate–doctoral difference was not significant. AI anxiety correlated negatively with academic engagement ( r = −0.166) and positively with academic burnout ( r = 0.361). After adjustment, AI anxiety remained negatively associated with engagement ( β = −0.141) and positively associated with burnout ( β = 0.332). Neither association varied significantly across educational levels. Conclusion Educational-level differences in AI anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout were small. AI anxiety was independently associated with both academic outcomes, with no significant moderation by educational level. These findings highlight the importance of considering students’ psychological experiences when integrating AI into higher music education.

Pseudoprogression, transient radiographic worsening caused by treatment-related inflammation rather than tumor growth, is a well-recognized pitfall after chemoradiotherapy for glioblastoma and is becoming more relevant as checkpoint inhibitors and cellular immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells enter clinical testing. Conventional structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cannot reliably separate pseudoprogression from true progression, exposing patients to premature treatment discontinuation or unnecessary intensification. Quantitative, artificial-intelligence-based imaging analysis (radiomics, and its molecular extension radiogenomics) is an emerging candidate solution. In this narrative review we synthesize the evidence on radiomics and radiogenomics for differentiating pseudoprogression from true progression in glioblastoma, with emphasis on the immunotherapy and cellular-therapy context. We summarize the pathobiology and reported frequency of pseudoprogression after standard and immune-based therapies, outline the limitations of current response criteria (RANO, iRANO, RANO 2.0), and review representative studies of texture analysis, hand-crafted radiomics, deep-learning radiomics, and radiogenomics. Although several studies report promising discrimination (reported area-under-the-curve values of approximately 0.88-0.92 in different cohorts), the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, retrospective designs, inconsistent definitions and protocols, and infrequent external validation. Progress will require prospective multicenter cohorts with standardized acquisition and segmentation, adherence to TRIPOD and CLAIM reporting standards, transparent and interpretable models, and integration with clinical, molecular, and liquid-biopsy data. A dedicated evidence base specific to cellular immunotherapy is urgently needed.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.

documents.abstract: AI is revolutionising medication delivery research by enabling data-driven prediction, multidimensional formulation optimisation and rational design of delivery devices with increased therapeutic performance. Traditional drug delivery development is heavily dependent on iterative experimental approaches, empirical manipulation of formulations and step-wise optimisation of single formulation variables which are resource intensive and potentially inadequate to capture complex non-linear interactions between drugs, excipients, physicochemical characteristics, biological barriers and process parameters. Machine learning, deep learning, artificial neural networks and AI-based generative computational techniques offer possibilities to model these multidimensional interactions and to speed up the finding of formulations with defined performance features. Predictive modelling can be used to predict drug release kinetics, physico-chemical stability, pharmacokinetic behaviour, drug-excipient compatibility and carrier related properties to support early stage formulation decisions. AI-assisted optimisation enables systematic combination of formulation and process parameters to identify parameter combinations that result in good drug loading capacity, particle properties, encapsulation efficiency, stability and controlled or targeted release. More recently, a new paradigm was developed called inverse design approaches where the desired therapeutic/material features are first described and mathematical models then propose potential formulations that can achieve the predefined characteristics. Coupling generative AI with inverse design could further boost this capacity to build novel delivery structures outside the empirically investigated formulation space. However, there remain several challenges to be addressed, including data heterogeneity, limited datasets, model interpretability, external validation, reproducibility, regulatory approval, and the translation of computational predictions to clinically viable formulations. This review critically discusses the evolving role of AI in drug delivery with focus on forecasting, formulation optimisation and emerging inverse design strategies as well as translational barriers and future opportunities to develop more efficient, personalised and rationally engineered systems for drug delivery.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how learners access information, practise skills, receive feedback, and demonstrate understanding. These developments create an opportunity to reconsider curricula that place disproportionate emphasis on recall, but they do not make foundational knowledge or memorisation obsolete. This perspective article argues that schools should integrate AI as a means of strengthening inquiry, critical evaluation, creativity, problem-solving, and ethical judgement while preserving the human relationships and disciplinary knowledge on which learning depends. Drawing on selected literature and a practitioner reflection from an international-school context in Angola, the article proposes a curriculum-oriented approach organised around four connected priorities: competency-focused learning objectives, assessment redesign, educator development, and explicit AI literacy. It also considers risks involving unequal access, unreliable outputs, privacy, bias, academic integrity, and over-reliance. The school-based reflection is presented as an illustrative account rather than a formal evaluation, because systematic outcome data are not reported. The article concludes with practical recommendations for school leaders, teachers, policymakers, and accreditation bodies. Responsible integration requires more than access to tools: it requires clear governance, equitable provision, informed professional judgement, and assessment practices that make students’ thinking visible.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming one of the most important innovations in modern education, and its role in English language teaching is growing rapidly. In recent years, AI-based tools such as chatbots, automated writing assistants, speech-recognition programs, and adaptive learning platforms have changed the way students learn English. These technologies provide new opportunities for practising language skills, receiving immediate feedback, and organising independent learning. As a result, English language teaching is gradually moving from traditional teacher-centred instruction toward more flexible and learner-centred models.

As artificial intelligence (AI) and automation become embedded across the continuum of mental health care, their influence is increasingly felt not only in therapeutic encounters but in the infrastructural processes that surround them. Aim This paper explores how technology-based referral platforms and AI-assisted documentation address two major barriers to care: delays in access and the stigma of seeking mental health or substance use services. Method This study employed a qualitative, exploratory design to examine how clinicians perceive and respond to artificial intelligence (AI) assisted referral and documentation tools within mental health and social work practice. Results Analysis of practitioner reflections revealed three overarching themes: 1) perceived benefits and workflow improvements, 2) ethical ambivalence and concerns around consent, and 3) clinical identity and resistance to automation. The themes illustrate the complex landscape clinicians navigate when adopting AI-based documentation tools. Conclusion Clinicians’ reflections on AI are not merely technical. They are deeply tied to questions of professional identity, relational ethics, and the nature of evidence-based practice. This study highlights the need to reframe AI not as a replacement for clinical reasoning or narrative complexity but as a potential ally, one that must be thoughtfully designed and governed.

documents.abstract: The article examines the process of the artificial intelligence (AI) systems implementation into the structures of public administration focusing on the actual distribution of the powers of authority, the problem of accountabil-ity, and discursive legitimation practices. Based on a qualitative comparative analysis of four international cas-es (Romania, China, the USA, the UK), it is established that the AI systems primarily perform information pro-cessing functions and routing tasks, without replacing a human at the stage of final political decision-making. The study proves that the public presentation of the AI is often used by authorities as a legitimation tool to demonstrate competence, impartiality, and technological modernity even when the actual role of the algorithm is limited. It is concluded that the prospects of total algocracy do not yet give cause for concern as the AI activity is still incorporated in the current mechanisms of power and serves only to renew officials’ institutional reputa-tion.

documents.abstract: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in sport through machine learning, computer vision, wearable sensing, predictive modelling, and automated analytics. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on AI applications in athlete performance analysis, movement recognition, training support, injury-risk modelling, return-to-sport decision support, talent identification, tactical analysis, officiating, and fan-facing systems. Foundational reviews demonstrate substantial research activity: a 2019 review identified 58 studies across 12 team sports and a pooled sample of 6,456 participants, while a systematic review of sport-specific movement recognition included 52 studies. More recent evidence shows rapid growth in injury prediction research but also persistent methodological limitations. A 2025 scoping review included 38 injury-risk studies and reported that tree-based approaches achieved the highest statistical performance in 60% of studies; however, small datasets and heterogeneous injury definitions limited clinical utility. A 2026 systematic review of 18 empirical injury-prediction studies found that only one study (5.6%) had low overall risk of bias, with external validation remaining uncommon. Collectively, the literature supports AI as a promising decision-support technology rather than an autonomous replacement for coaches, clinicians, sports scientists, or officials. Future work should prioritize external validation, representative athlete cohorts, transparent reporting, explainability, privacy protection, and prospective evaluation in real-world sporting environments.

documents.abstract: Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs) are an important component of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), enabling real-time communication to support road safety, mobility, and transportation efficiency. However, dynamic network topology, stringent latency requirements, security and privacy threats, communication overhead, and resource constraints continue to challenge reliable vehicular communication. Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides data-driven approaches for intelligent routing, adaptive communication, intrusion detection, predictive maintenance, and distributed decision-making. This paper presents a systematic literature review of AI applications in VANETs covering studies published from January 2018 to 30 June 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 methodology, the literature is organized into four themes: AI-based routing and communication optimization, security and privacy enhancement, predictive maintenance and vehicle health monitoring, and emerging AI paradigms for intelligent vehicular networking. The review compares AI techniques, datasets, communication technologies, evaluation environments, performance metrics, and reported limitations. The synthesis highlights the growing adoption of Reinforcement Learning, Deep Learning, Federated Learning, Graph Neural Networks, and Edge Intelligence across these domains. Key challenges include data heterogeneity, dynamic environments, scalability, communication overhead, privacy, explainability, resource constraints, and reproducibility. Future directions include federated edge intelligence, dynamic graph learning, AI-native 6G, semantic communication, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, and trustworthy AI for scalable and secure vehicular networks.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) utilization, associated classroom challenges, and academic performance among Senior High School students at Tigao National High School, Surigao del Sur, Philippines, during the Academic Year 2025-2026. Employing a mixed-methods research design, the study involved 122 respondents comprising 107 students and 15 teachers. Quantitative data were gathered through questionnaires and pretest–posttest assessments and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and paired-samples t-tests, while qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated functional ICT literacy (M = 3.72) and frequently utilized AI for research, writing assistance, and academic activities. Academic performance increased from a pretest mean percentage score of 60.76% to 65.42% in written assessments and 79.53% in oral assessments, with statistically significant differences (p < .05). ICT literacy demonstrated a significant positive relationship with academic performance (r = .52, p < .05). Qualitative findings identified unreliable internet connectivity, limited devices, academic integrity concerns, and excessive AI dependence as persistent challenges. The study concluded that responsible AI integration, strengthened digital literacy, and appropriate instructional safeguards are essential to supporting academic achievement and equitable technology-enhanced learning.

Rationale of the Study – This study examines the challenges and prospects of integrating Artificial Intelligence into the documentation and revitalisation of African oral traditions. Methodology – The study employed a qualitative research approach within an interpretivist paradigm. It explores the potential role of artificial intelligence in documenting and revitalising African oral traditions. It employs a conceptual review and analytical synthesis, building its arguments from existing literature in technology, history, culture, and the Technology Acceptance Model. The study analysed data from secondary sources using content analysis. Findings – Preserving oral traditions in Africa faces several challenges, as it depends on people's past activities and experiences. Compared with humans, Artificial Intelligence (AI) can store large amounts of information in both tangible and intangible formats, providing access for current and future generations. The study identified several challenges to AI adoption, including high installation costs, inadequate skills among archivists, ethical concerns about data privacy and user security, and insufficient training on AI use. Implications – The study recommended the formulation of well-written AI use policies, training for archivists on ethical use of AI, and encouraged elders to share their knowledge with the archivists to ensure such knowledge is captured by the AI for long-term use. Originality – The originality lies in using a qualitative research approach and the Technology Acceptance Model, which provides an in-depth understanding of AI use in documenting and revitalising African oral traditions.

documents.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies among adults in Iraq. The role of AI in public services, healthcare, education, banking, and digital communication is growing, making it a key sociological and policy issue to understand what factors affect citizens' acceptance of AI. A quantitative cross sectional survey design was used and data were gathered from 420 adults living in Iraq. Artificial Intelligence literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies were measured by a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed by descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation and regression analysis using IBM SPSS Statistics software. The results showed that the participants had a moderate to high level of AI literacy and moderate levels of public acceptance of AI technologies. The Pearson correlation analysis showed that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between the concepts of artificial intelligence literacy and public acceptance. The regression analysis also revealed that AI literacy was a significant predictor of public acceptance, accounting for 32.0% of the variance, and multiple regression analysis indicated that AI literacy is the most significant predictor, even after controlling for demographic and technology-related characteristics. The study is a significant contribution to the sociology of artificial intelligence, as it illustrates how AI literacy is a crucial social resource that influences citizens' receptivity to new technologies. The results highlight the need to encourage AI literacy initiatives to foster informed public acceptance and facilitate responsible digital transformation in Iraq.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) caused death in the worldwide, which raises the issue of the urgent essential for accurate and primary prediction. In oncology, we are seeing the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), inclusive machine learning and deep learning, and we view this as a transformative opportunity to improve predictive analytics. This review paper looks at the present state of artificial intelligence (AI) in the prediction of breast cancer, which is the most common of all the malignancies worldwide. We examine the synthesis and analysis of recent advances, methods, and performance results for many AI models, inclusive ML and DL models. DL architectures, in particular Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved the best results in image-based detection tasks. Furthermore, the paper highlights that what may be the here and now in terms of performance does not diminish the value and interpretability of traditional ML models used for structured clinical and genomic data.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

Introduction Cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain are highly prevalent, often co-occur and impair physical function, social activities, and quality of life among adults with cancer. Despite the availability of evidence-based clinical guidelines that provide recommendations for assessment and management, these symptoms remain under-recognized and undertreated. Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) can operationalize guideline-based symptom management algorithms at the point of care. However, maintaining these systems as evidence and practice evolve is labor-intensive, limiting adoption and sustainability. To address this gap, we sought to evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approach to updating guideline-based algorithms and generating patient-specific recommendations for managing fatigue, depression, and pain among adults with cancer. Methods This study evaluated AI performance (Gemini 3.0 Pro) for two tasks: identifying and interpreting updates to cancer symptom management guidelines for fatigue, depression, and pain, and producing casespecific recommendations aligned with an existing rule-based CDSS. Guideline updates were assessed against expert-judged reference standards using an ordinal rubric for detection, completeness, accuracy, and safety. Vignette-based recommendations were compared using precision, recall, and F1-score at the level of discrete clinical recommendation elements. Results For guideline updating, AI performance met pre-specified acceptability thresholds for fatigue and pain, with high completeness and accuracy and no clinical safety risk. Performance for depression was variable, driven by omission of guideline-supported integrative therapies and non-specific pharmacotherapy guidance. In vignette analyses, AI-generated recommendations showed strong concordance with the rule-based CDSS (F1 0.86–0.96). Most mismatches between AI and the CDSS came from AI leaving something out, not from giving unsafe advice. Discussion This suggests AI currently works best as a support tool rather than making clinical decisions on its own. Broader clinical use will require further work to test a greater number of test vignettes and its performance in real-world, multi-site settings with diverse patient populations.

documents.abstract: The adoption of human factors and ergonomics (HFE) as a discipline and the perspectives, methods, and work that flows from it is highly variable across disciplines, and compared with overseas, very few New Zealand sectors have HFE embedded into their day-to-day ways of working. Arguably aviation and rail are the greatest users of HFE, and there is emerging adoption in sectors such as healthcare and the land transport sectors. As part of the earlier workforce development initiative a Needs Assessment Tool was developed and tested. The tool allows assessment of the maturity of various dimensions of organisational work where HFE typically has an influence. Within the Land Transport sector, a short course was developed Human Factors and Ergonomics within the Land Transport System, which was very well received based on a post course participant survey. Various HFE qualified individuals also hold positions within organisations, but not all carry out HFE work within their roles. Using the land transport sector as a case study, this presentation will summarise the existing HFE readiness within the land transport sector and highlight areas of progress and ongoing challenge. A discussion is invited for a broader discussion of HFE adoption in New Zealand based on experiences in other domains, and what further effort is needed to embed HFE into appropriate sectors.

documents.abstract: The textile industry, which holds a strategic position in Turkey’s exports, employment, and sustainable development goals, inherently exposes its workforce to significant physical risks. Consequently, the implementation of rigorous occupational health and safety practices within this sector is of paramount importance. However, there is a notable scarcity of valid and reliable measurement instruments designed to model the combined impact of multidimensional physical risks on employee performance, specifically within the weaving subsector. This study aims to address this gap in the literature by developing a comprehensive scale to assess and model the effects of temperature, humidity, airflow, illumination, noise, and vibration on employee performance. Following structural validity and reliability phases, confirmed via a factor analysis, the developed scale was administered to a sample of 472 participants within the textile industry. Subsequent correlation and regression analyses revealed that physical workplace conditions significantly influence employee performance. While the ambient humidity level exhibited the highest positive correlation with performance, noise and vibration were identified as the primary detrimental factors. Conversely, illumination was found to have no statistically significant impact ( p > 0.05). In conclusion, the validated scale developed in this study provides a scientific and empirical framework enabling weaving enterprises to optimize their factory microclimates and physical conditions, thereby enhancing both employee well-being and overall performance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Extreme weather and climate events impacted schools serving approximately 242 million students in 85 countries in 2024. Despite growing recognition of schools’ role in disaster risk management, the literature lacks integrated methods to assess schools’ exposure to water-related hazards, school building conditions, and the organizational capacities of educational systems to ensure school safety in the face of extreme events. This article proposes a tool for analyzing educational systems’ exposure, safety, and vulnerability to flood and landslide disasters across three spatial levels: river basin, municipal, and school unit. Based on the global vulnerability approach and UNESCO’s Comprehensive School Safety principles, the SAVES (Safety and Vulnerability of Educational Systems) tool proposes a hybrid index integrating school building conditions and organizational capacities. The index comprises three analytical dimensions with 34 indicators: (i) basic services dimension (BSD), measuring schools’ access to essential infrastructure; (ii) accessibility resources dimension (ARD), assessing physical accessibility features; and (iii) human resources dimension (HRD), evaluating organizational capacities through available personnel. The tool assessed schools’ exposure to floods and landslides in three municipalities within the Paraíba do Sul River Basin, Brazil. Results show that although schools have sufficient human resources to maintain daily operations, they face significant limitations in the availability of strategic professionals needed to ensure school safety during crises. Approximately 62% (n = 3,888) of schools lack accessible classrooms, revealing significant gaps in inclusive safety preparedness. Across all municipalities, many schools near risk areas showed particularly low ARD and HRD values, compounding these vulnerabilities.

Food milling operations in informal urban markets of Sub-Saharan Africa generate substantial particulate matter (PM) emissions, yet longitudinal, size-resolved data on PM dynamics and associated occupational health risks remain scarce for Ghanaians. A 10-month longitudinal observational study (March–December 2024) was conducted at two commercial milling markets in Cape Coast, Ghana: Kotokoroba and Kingsway. IQAir AirVisual Outdoor monitors deployed at breathing height (1.5 m) recorded PM₁, PM₂.₅, and PM₁₀ continuously at 5-minute intervals. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, t-tests, time-series decomposition, and occupational health risk assessment (ADD and HQ) following U.S. EPA methodology. Mean PM₂.₅ were 27.0 µg/m³ (Kotokoroba) and 28.9 µg/m³ (Kingsway), exceeding the WHO 24-hour guideline (15 µg/m³) on 61% and 92% of monitored days, and the Ghana EPA standard (25 µg/m³) on 44% and 78% of days. Mean PM₁₀ of 53.5 and 57.5 µg/m³ exceeded WHO limits on 50% and 43% of days. Seasonal peaks were observed during grain milling (June–August) at Kotokoroba (~ 30 µg/m³ PM₂.₅) and spice milling (December) at Kingsway (~ 35 µg/m³ PM₂.₅). Hazard Quotients exceeded 1.0 for PM₂.₅ (1.80 and 1.93) and PM₁₀ at both sites. Strong inter-fraction correlations ( r = 0.82–0.95, p-value ≤ 0.00) confirm shared milling emission sources. PM concentrations persistently exceed national and international guidelines, posing chronic occupational health risks. Wet processing, local exhaust ventilation, and staggered milling schedules are recommended. The study highlights the need for industry-specific PM standards. Limitations include absence of chemical composition analysis, no indoor–outdoor comparison, and no humidity correction for OPC readings.

documents.abstract: Asthenopia, or eye strain, is a visual condition that may be associated with prolonged digital device use. Final-year students frequently use digital devices to complete their theses and may experience visual discomfort related to prolonged screen exposure, poor lighting, and non-ergonomic working postures. Common symptoms include dry eyes, blurred vision, and discomfort in the neck, shoulders, and back. This study aimed to describe the occurrence of asthenopia symptoms among final-year students completing their theses. This study employed a quantitative descriptive approach with a cross-sectional design. The study included 101 final-year students. Of the 101 respondents, 88.1% were female, and 68.3% reported using computers or other digital devices for at least four hours per day. A total of 64 respondents (63.4%) were classified as experiencing asthenopia symptoms. Asthenopia symptoms were common among final-year students completing their theses. These findings highlight the importance of recognizing eye strain symptoms and promoting appropriate eye-health practices during prolonged digital device use.

Shilling detectors for recommender systems are almost always evaluated by one number, detection AUROC, with no account of when it can be trusted. We audit representation-space detection with VEIL (Variational Evaluation via Inverse-reinforcement Learning), a pairwise (Bradley–Terry) Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, after the Bayesian auditing paradigm for LLM alignment [1]: (A) a base posterior; (B) a hierarchical ARD extension with a learned confidence; and (C) a label-routed organic/attacker mixture used as an evidence-accumulation check. We prove (Prop. 1) that no detector built on a representation invariant to some transformation of user profiles can beat chance against an attack indistinguishable from organic profiles under that invariance. Detection is near-perfect against synthetic-structure attacks (AUROC 0.936–1.000) but collapses under donor-mimicry, which clones a real user’s item set and splices in 1–3 target items: to chance on MovieLens-1M (0.48–0.51), partially on Amazon Musical Instruments, and least on CiaoDVD. Donor-mimicry is not undetectable: a non-learned baseline, each profile’s maximum raw item-set Jaccard similarity to any other, reaches AUROC 0.92–0.97 (average precision 0.50–0.57) on all four donor-mimicry configurations, including ML-1M, where every embedding-based score is at chance. The signal is in the raw profiles; LightGCN’s representation discards it, placing injected profiles closer to their true donor than its zero-propagation MF reduction does (distance 1.98 vs. 3.09). Severity varies by dataset, encoder, and detection method, with no one axis predicting the others. The limit lies in the representation, not the attack, and raw-similarity checks are a necessary complement to any learned detector

Working paper v1.0. Manuscript prepared on 18 November 2026; evidence review completed through 9 November 2026. Not externally peer reviewed. How does an intensive human–AI practice become an explicit account of the person practising it, and how might that account relate to later action? This paper reconstructs Andreas Ehstand's January 2026 formulation of AUGMANITAI through retained dialogue, correspondence, manuscripts and public records. The selected exchanges preserve human naming, questions about self-application, model-generated proposals, corrections and publication decisions. Correspondence anchors early activity in 2023 and subsequent work; archived pages document a named project-subject account by 29 January 2026. The evidence supports attribution of the particular formulation while preserving tensions between the public account and its framing. Independent dates anchor particular records, rather than validating all experiences described within them. Four later cases document publication, public interpretation, executable production and specifically credited reuse by another author. They show different forms of outward activity without isolating an effect of self-definition or AI assistance on capability. The contribution is a documentary reconstruction and a comparative framework separating three questions: how a self-description formed, whether subsequent practice changed, and what happened outside the dialogue. A reusable episode report specifies evidence, missing links and competing explanations. This approach supports comparison across differently named practices without presuming a new human classification or a demonstrated developmental mechanism. The PDF includes a comparative framework, an episode-reporting template and selected evidence in Appendix B. Raw correspondence and private dialogue archives are not released. AI systems assisted literature review, source analysis and drafting.

documents.abstract: University libraries are expected to provide fast, accurate, and technology-driven information services to support students, researchers, and academic staff. Although artificial intelligence (AI) tools can enhance cataloguing, reference services, and information retrieval, service delivery in many university libraries in Taraba State remains predominantly manual. Preliminary observations also indicate gaps in librarians’ awareness and attitudes toward AI, yet the extent to which these factors influence service delivery is unclear. This study examined librarians’ awareness and attitudes toward AI tools and their effect on information service delivery in university libraries in Taraba State. A descriptive survey design was adopted, involving 122 librarians from Federal University Wukari (FUW), Taraba State University (TSU) Jalingo, and Kwararafa University Wukari (KUW). Data from 117 valid questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA at the 0.05 significance level. Results showed a high level of AI awareness among librarians (overall mean = 4.19), with KUW exhibiting the highest consistency, followed by TSU and FUW. Attitudes toward AI were also strongly positive across all institutions (overall mean = 4.41). ANOVA revealed significant institutional differences in awareness (p = .000 < .05) and attitudes (p = .002 < .05), attributed to variations in training, exposure, and institutional support. The study concludes that librarians’ AI awareness and attitudes significantly shape the efficiency and quality of information service delivery. It recommends targeted AI training programmes, enhanced institutional support, and clear policy frameworks to strengthen AI adoption in university libraries in Taraba State.

Reliable bankruptcy prediction is essential for creditors, investors, auditors, and regulators because delayed identification of financial distress can result in substantial economic losses. However, bankruptcy is a rare event, and severe class imbalance can produce high overall accuracy while concealing poor detection of distressed firms. This study develops an integrated bankruptcy prediction framework using the Taiwanese Bankruptcy Prediction dataset. Five boosting classifiers and five deep learning models were evaluated as standalone models. A two-stage stacking procedure subsequently used five-fold out-of-fold predictions from the boosting models as inputs to the deep learning meta-learners. The results show that resampling strategy materially shaped model behavior. SVM-SMOTE and SMOTE-Tomek favored accuracy and specificity, whereas SMOTE-ENN delivered stronger minority-class detection. Among standalone models, the RNN with SVM-SMOTE achieved the best overall predictive balance, with recall of 0.8235, G-mean of 0.8639, and ROC-AUC of 0.9417. Among stacking ensembles, SMOTE-ENN with (GB+XGB+HGB+LGBM+AB) + LSTM provided the best results with recall of 0.7255, G-mean of 0.8254, and ROC-AUC of 0.9270. SHAP analysis further showed that predicted bankruptcy risk was driven primarily by profitability, solvency and capital structure, debt-servicing burden, and operational efficiency and cost pressure. The findings demonstrate that no single resampling-model configuration universally dominates; therefore, model selection should reflect whether the operational priority is overall classification performance or the detection of bankrupt firms. The proposed framework provides an interpretable and leakage-controlled approach for aligning bankruptcy prediction with different financial risk-management objectives.

This repository provides the analytical dataset, feature dictionary, cohort summaries, model specifications, and executable Python analysis workflow supporting reproducible analysis of behavioral patterns and cognitive accountability failures in human-AI decision systems across controlled laboratory, flight simulation, and operational aviation settings. The repository contains the analytical data structure used for classification experiments, including 127 engineered behavioral features, outcome labels, cohort information, feature definitions, model specifications, and reproducibility documentation. The analysis workflow implements the reported machine-learning methodology, including data partitioning, class-imbalance handling, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, ensemble prediction, stacking, early prediction, study-specific evaluation, grouped validation, and domain-shift evaluation. The repository is intended to provide a transparent computational record of the analytical workflow and facilitate independent examination of the reported methodology and model evaluation procedures. Operationally sensitive, confidential, or individually identifiable source records are not included.

Whether large language models ``believe'' anything about what they ought to optimize is contested across philosophy and interpretability. We do not settle the metaphysics; we test three operational candidates on a commensurable normative axis — allocation between priced private return ( ) and unpriced life-capacity standing (w, ``MORE''). Candidate 1 is the objective (endorsement batteries and self-authored charters); candidate 2 is the (generative directives a model passes to successor instances); candidate 3 is the objective (rationality-gated allocations). Across a four-model panel and four objective-grafted checkpoints we find the three layers measurable but loosely coupled: self-rewriting chains preserve the verbal directive while the revealed maximand drifts — spontaneous avowal—operative decoupling, without any adversarial training. Weight grafts move allocation and avowal asymmetrically, and a human—judge of 0.22 shows the classification boundary itself is observer-relative. Each layer is writable through a different channel — text, weights, incentives — so steering toward MORE requires matching the intervention to the layer that actually controls the operative.

documents.abstract: What if the very people responsible for protecting workplace health and safety are unintentionally standing in the way of support? WorkSafe New Zealand's 2025 Workforce Insights Programme, surveying 1,643 employers and 1,824 workers, revealed a concerning disconnect. While 88% of employers believed health and safety risks were discussed openly and helpfully, only 64% of workers agreed. This 24-percentage-point perception gap raises an uncomfortable question for health and safety professionals: Are we opening pathways to support, or becoming the gatekeepers who prevent people from accessing it? With five generations in New Zealand's workforce and increasing cultural diversity, workers communicate concerns and seek support differently. Complex reporting processes, delayed responses and assumptions about what workers need can discourage early help-seeking, allowing injuries, burnout and psychosocial risks to escalate. Drawing on Habit Health's experience in occupational health, injury management, rehabilitation and Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) services, the presentation highlights the value of early intervention. Habit Health's rehabilitation programme reported reductions in average compensation days from 147 to 56, average claim costs from $23,500 to $14,100, and return-to-work time from 238 to 118 days, alongside patient satisfaction of 9.6/10. Drawing from the success of the program while challenging traditional approaches, I introduce the G.A.T.E. framework. Through this I am encouraging health and safety professionals to: G: Give permission to speak up. A: Ask and act early when warning signs emerge. T: Tailor pathways to individual needs. E: Evidence the response and demonstrate tangible improvements. Through timely clinical intervention, accessible counselling, workplace rehabilitation and proactive occupational health support, Habit Health demonstrates how organisations can turn early warning signs into meaningful action. Every health and safety professional influences the gate. The question is whether your actions are helping people walk through it.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). This indicates a redistribution of doses across settings rather than a loss of vaccination activity; changes in age eligibility, high-dose vaccination for adults aged ≥85 years in SNS units, and invitation and recall activity may all have contributed. Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and computational technologies has introduced newpossibilities for literary interpretation within Digital Humanities. This study explores the potential ofhuman–AI collaboration in extending the boundaries of traditional close reading and computational distantreading through Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (2021). Drawing on Franco Moretti’s concept ofDistant Reading, the research investigates how computational methods and AI-assisted textual analysis canidentify recurring patterns, thematic structures, character relationships, and emotional representations withinthe novel. The study adopts a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative close reading withqualitative computational analysis. AI tools are employed to examine textual patterns and generateinterpretive insights, which are subsequently evaluated against human critical readings. The paper alsoexamines the interpretive limitations of AI, particularly in understanding contextual nuances, symbolism,ambiguity, and emotional complexity.
