Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has created new opportunitiesfor personalised, adaptive, and learner-centred instruction. However, multilingual learners in Indiaencounter distinctive challenges arising from linguistic diversity, unequal language proficiency,mother-tongue interference, and differences in educational backgrounds. Although conventional AIpowered personalisation provides individualised content and feedback, it often prioritises immediateperformance improvement rather than developing learners’ awareness of their own learning processes.To address this limitation, the present study proposes Metacognitive AI Scaffolding as an innovativepedagogical approach that moves beyond personalisation toward conscious, reflective, and selfregulated English language learning. The study examines how AI-based scaffolding can supportmultilingual learners in planning, monitoring, evaluating, and regulating their language-learningstrategies. Using a qualitative, conceptual research methodology, the study draws on existing literatureon artificial intelligence in education, metacognition, scaffolding, multilingual pedagogy, and selfregulated learning. It explores the potential of AI tools to provide reflective prompts, diagnosticfeedback, guided questioning, and adaptive learning support while recognising learners’ multilingualbackgrounds. The proposed framework seeks to reposition AI from a content-delivery mechanism toa metacognitive learning partner. Ultimately, the study contributes to an inclusive and learner-centredframework for English language education in India by strengthening learner autonomy, criticalreflection, and multilingual competence.

Prison visitation is usually administered as a security operation, yet it is also a relational and rehabilitative intervention. Rule 58 of the Nelson Mandela Rules provides for regular contact with family and friends through correspondence, telecommunications and visits (United Nations, 2015). A meta-analysis of 16 studies associated visitation with a 26% reduction in recidivism, although effects varied by visit type, outcome, gender and follow-up (Mitchell et al., 2016). This is not a universal causal guarantee, but it shows that access to visitation is not a minor administrative convenience.Digital visitation can widen access for families separated by distance, cost, illness or disability. Video visits can help incarcerated fathers take part in children's daily lives, while raising problems of timing, technology and the absence of touch (Duursma et al., 2024;Hanley et al., 2024), and users may value remote access while still preferring in-person contact (Murdoch and King, 2020). Remote systems can also reduce agency, comprehension and privacy for people already disadvantaged (McKay and Macintosh, 2024). The appropriate policy is complementarity, not substitution. Video conferencing alone is not artificial intelligence (AI). We use AI-mediated visitation to mean pathways in which AI informs identity verification, scheduling, translation, risk flagging, content moderation, interruption or post-visit review. The 2026 UNODC-ICRC Handbook states that video visits should supplement in-person visits and that AI in prisons should be fair, explainable, contestable and under human control (UNODC and ICRC, 2026). We argue that these principles require a specific rule: AI may assist access and safety, but it should never be the sole basis for denying, suspending or terminating family contact.Transparency, accountability, auditing and human oversight are established principles (Kroll et al., 2017;Ananny and Crawford, 2018;UNESCO, 2021;OECD, 2024;Cheong, 2024), and the Council of Europe has already adapted them to prisons and probation (Council of Europe, 2024). We do not claim to originate them. Our contribution is to show where general frameworks stop short when the decision concerns family contact, and to supply three elements they lack.First, a consequence-tiered classification (Table 1) separates assistive functions from gatekeeping, interventional and inferential ones, so that safeguards scale with consequence rather than applying uniformly to "prison AI". Second, a relational-irreversibility criterion: a missed visit, a child's birthday call or a terminated conversation cannot be restored by a later appeal, so review must occur before or during the contact window. General frameworks treat remedy as retrospective; visitation requires prospective or same-session remedy. Third, third-party standing: visitors are not detainees, yet their faces, voices and devices are processed. Frameworks oriented to the detained person rarely give families an independent right to notice, correction and appeal. Rapid gains in AI capability do not settle these questions, because reliability, interpretability and evaluation remain open problems even in well-resourced scientific domains (Xu et al., 2026); they are harder still in a coercive setting with contested ground truth.We distinguish documented evidence from hypothetical scenarios; Supplementary Table S1 lists each source and its evidential status.A national survey of US video-visitation contracts found that 74% of jails adopting video visitation eliminated in-person visits, and some vendor contracts required this (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015). In England, a 2018-2019 trial scanned the faces of 770 visitors at HMP Humber; some visitors turned back on learning of the scans, and campaigners warned that deterring families would be counter-productive (Prison Legal News, 2019). During the COVID-19 pandemic, prisons in England and Wales introduced video calls using software with facial recognition (Ministry of Justice, 2020); family guidance at one prison warned that background photographs could disrupt recognition and end calls prematurely (HMP Forest Bank, 2020), and the supplier advertised emotion recognition to detect changes in mood (Made Purple Ltd, n.d.). In the United States, AI transcription and keyword alerting of prisoners' calls has been adopted by state and federal agencies, while families and advocates have raised concerns about misinterpretation and racial bias (Route Fifty, 2021;Correctional News, 2026). Outside prisons, Australia's Robodebt inquiry showed how automated decisions without adequate human review can cause serious and widespread harm (Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, 2023).A visitor whose face fails verification on a poor-quality phone camera is refused a call with no manual alternative; an emotion-inference flag labels a crying child's conversation "agitated" and prompts termination. We present these as scenarios that the documented features above make plausible, not as reported incidents.The framework does not pretend these values align. Security versus rights: contraband and witness intimidation are real, but a system optimised only for detected incidents is misspecified, because its costs, such as false rejections, deterred visits and abandoned contact, fall on families, who already face burdensome visiting procedures (Boppre et al., 2022), and are rarely measured. Efficiency versus oversight: automation saves staff time precisely by reducing human scrutiny, and reviewers tend to defer to automated alerts (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010); nominal oversight can then legitimise unreliable outputs (Green, 2022). Transparency versus gaming: full disclosure of detection rules may help circumvention, yet a bare reference to "security reasons" prevents correction and undermines legitimacy (Tyler, 2006). We resolve this by requiring an individual, actionable reason and disclosure of decision rules to an independent auditor even where public disclosure is limited. Public duty versus commercial incentive: where vendors are paid per call or per minute, contract terms can shape visitation policy (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015), so procurement is itself a governance instrument.Table 1 specifies, for each tier, minimum safeguards, appeal routes, review timelines, audit duties and measurable fairness indicators. Three features carry the argument. Appeals are two-stage: an on-site supervisor with authority to override decisions within the same session, followed by written review within 72 hours or before the next scheduled visit, whichever is sooner, with escalation to a body independent of the prison. Accountability is named: each consequential deployment has a responsible official, tamperevident decision logs, and contracts that prohibit in-person bans and guarantee auditor access to data. Fairness is measured through disaggregated false-rejection rates, override rates and appeal outcomes, with predefined disparity thresholds that trigger suspension pending review. This treats trustworthiness as a lifecycle responsibility rather than a launch certificate (Tabassi, 2023). The numerical values in Table 1 are proposed starting points for calibration, not validated standards.Three red lines follow the irreversibility criterion. No adverse visitation decision may rest solely on AI output; biometric failure must trigger an alternative verification route rather than exclusion; and speech, behaviour or emotion inference must never be treated as established misconduct. Where immediate intervention is necessary for safety, it should be temporary, documented, proportionate and promptly reviewed.These requirements will land differently. In the European Union, the AI Act classifies emotion recognition and many biometric and law-enforcement uses as high-risk and gives affected persons a right to an explanation, yet its prohibition of emotion recognition covers workplaces and education, not detention (European Union, 2024). Malaysia has no AI-specific statute; its national AI governance guidelines are voluntary (MOSTI, 2024), and its Personal Data Protection Act 2010 does not apply to federal and state governments (Malaysia, 2010). Its prison service already combines online booking with in-person and video visits (Berita Harian, 2024), so AI could be added without a dedicated legal framework. In the United States, visitation technology is often procured county by county (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015), and familyengagement policies differ markedly between states (Pappas et al., 2024).Resources also differ. We therefore propose a minimum floor applicable everywhere, consisting of the red lines, a non-digital route, same-session human override and incident logging, and an enhanced tier of independent audits, disaggregated reporting and impact assessment for systems with adequate capacity. Where independent review bodies are absent, an existing ombudsman, inspectorate or human-rights commission can be designated. Low capacity justifies restricting AI to assistive functions; it does not justify weaker safeguards for gatekeeping ones.The framework is normative and should be tested. We propose five questions.• RQ1. Do false-rejection rates of biometric visitor verification differ by age, skin tone, disability and device quality, and does a manual fallback close the resulting gap in completed visits? Laboratory testing already shows demographic differentials across face-recognition algorithms (Grother et al., 2019). Design: disaggregated audit of operational logs.• RQ2. Does introducing an AI-assisted pathway change completed visits, cancellations and inperson visit numbers? Design: stepped-wedge rollout across facilities. • RQ3. How often do reviewers override automated flags, and does this change with time pressure and access to underlying evidence? Design: log analysis of staff interviews. • RQ4. Which explanation formats enable families to identify and correct errors? Design:randomised vignette experiments with visitors. • RQ5. Does same-session review reduce irreversible relational harm compared with retrospective appeal? Design: comparison of family-reported visit quality and appeal outcomes across sites.Evaluation should combine security indicators with relational and procedural outcomes, report who is excluded, and involve incarcerated people and families in defining success.AI is not inherently incompatible with humane visitation. It may reduce delays, improve translation and extend contact when travel is impossible. The test is institutional purpose and the affected person's practical capacity to understand, challenge and correct an outcome before relational harm becomes irreversible. Preserve in-person visitation; use video to expand contact; tier AI functions by consequence; prohibit solely automated adverse decisions; and measure success by whether families keep safe, dignified and meaningful contact.

documents.abstract: Human Factors (HF) practitioners can be drawn to the more visible aspects of the discipline: end user engagement, task analysis, usability assessment, design innovation etc. Lesser attention is given to the less glamorous, and often less celebrated, work that occurs after the data collection is concluded and the analyse is complete. Yet for many HF practitioners, a significant proportion of HF effort can be dedicated to reporting, assurance, issue management, compliance demonstration, audit responses, and evidence gathering. These activities are sometimes perceived as administrative overheads rather than core HF practice. This presentation challenges that perception.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

Course-aligned artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly offered as learning support in higher education. Beyond providing practice and feedback, they may also help teachers identify gaps in understanding across a cohort. In a second-year medical microbiology and immunology unit of 500 to 800 students, a course-aligned AI assistant built on The University of Sydney’s Cogniti platform gave students scenario-based short-answer practice with rubric-referenced feedback. Its conversation logs turned out to be a diagnostic instrument. Across more than 1300 conversations, the logs revealed cohort-level knowledge gaps and recurring terminology errors mid-semester. An exploratory analysis also found small positive correlations between practice-oriented use of the assistant and final short-answer marks, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously. The gaps were fed back to the class through an interactive revision resource used in lectures. These insights could be obtained through three approaches requiring different levels of technical expertise: the platform’s own no-code summaries, method-led coding with basic programming, and specialist computational analysis. We also discuss how the approach can be adapted where no equivalent platform exists. The project highlights that a course-aligned AI assistant can provide valuable insight into cohort-level understanding of the subject.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative AI into design education generates tensions between innovation and pedagogy. This paper presents a pilot program that combines structured spaces for practical learning and critical reflection on generative AI. Implemented within a large undergraduate Storytelling and Animation course, the program combined seamless AI-based creative exercises with a deliberately seamful activity intended to disrupt automation and foreground human agency. By analysing student reflections collected through written reports, we find that this pedagogical program can foster diverse critical positionings, enabling students to negotiate authorship, question tool dependencies, and reappropriate creative processes. Rather than adopting or rejecting generative AI uncritically, students developed nuanced understandings of its role in their design practices. The main contribution of this work is to foreground the combination of seamless and seamful activities as a pedagogical tactic for teaching practical competences while encouraging critical reflexivity about the integration of generative AI into higher education.

Introduction Female athletes train in settings where the body serves at once as an instrument of performance and as an object of evaluation. Whether body appreciation relates to the quality of sport participation motivation, and through which psychological route, remains underexamined. Drawing on objectification theory and self-determination theory, this study tested whether objectified body consciousness, operationalized as body surveillance and body shame, statistically accounts for that association, and whether the first stage of the indirect route differs between aesthetic and non-aesthetic sports. Methods Chinese female university athletes ( N = 452; 201 aesthetic, 251 non-aesthetic) from six universities in Henan and Xinjiang completed the Body Appreciation Scale-2, the Objectified Body Consciousness Scale, and the intrinsic motivation subscale of the Sport Motivation Scale-II. Confirmatory factor analysis and tests of configural, metric, and scalar measurement invariance preceded the estimation of a first-stage moderated mediation model (PROCESS Model 7) with 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Results The four-factor measurement model fit acceptably, χ 2 (371) = 651.54, χ 2 /df = 1.76, CFI = 0.960, TLI = 0.956, RMSEA = 0.041, SRMR = 0.049, and invariance held across sport type (all |ΔCFI| < = 0.004). Higher body appreciation went together with higher intrinsic motivation (total B = 0.650, p < 0.001), and objectified body consciousness carried part of that association. Its negative link with body appreciation was stronger in aesthetic sports (interaction B = −0.358, p < 0.001, Δ R 2 = 0.024), giving conditional indirect associations of 0.284 [95% CI (0.200, 0.385)] and 0.100 [95% CI (0.036, 0.166)]; the index of moderated mediation was 0.185 [95% CI (0.089, 0.295)]. Two alternative orderings of the same variables fitted worse or reversed the sign pattern. Discussion Body appreciation is a relevant correlate of motivational quality in women’s sport, and the appearance-saturated climate of aesthetic disciplines merits particular applied attention. This design is cross-sectional and each category aggregates heterogeneous disciplines, so these implications remain provisional pending longitudinal and experimental verification.

Deep-learning classifiers for breast ultrasound are usually evaluated on images from their training institution, and self-supervised foundation models are increasingly proposed as more transferable than supervised networks; whether ranking ability, decision thresholds, and probability calibration survive a change in institution has rarely been tested under leakage-controlled conditions. We fine-tuned ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, a supervised Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16), and self-supervised DINOv2 under one shared protocol on the official BUS-BRA five-fold partitions, each fold with three seeds, and on three case-grouped hold-out splits, and evaluated every trained model unchanged on the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset. The supervised models largely retained their discrimination externally. ResNet-50 had the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve under the official folds, but no criterion separated it from ViT-B/16, whose small hold-out advantage at the decision threshold did not recur. In every official-fold run, both models labeled a larger share of BUSI than of BUS-BRA images malignant, although prevalence was the same—a shift that temperature scaling cannot correct. Top-label calibration error also understated malignant-class miscalibration. Full-frame DINOv2 did not fit its training data in any run, although exploratory lesion cropping produced good discrimination. External evaluations should report operating-point transport and class-wise calibration alongside discrimination.

In workplace learning (WPL) research, workplace affordances concern possibilities for participation and learning that arise in relation to people, work practices and their social and material arrangements. These possibilities vary across professional groups and circumstances, while learning also depends on how individuals engage in work. This article proposes a tentative framework for analysing that variation by bringing Billett’s (2001) account of co-participation into dialogue with Davis and Chouinard’s (2017) theorisation of affordances. It adapts six mechanisms – request, demand, allow, encourage, discourage and refuse – to examine how possibilities for participation are shaped in workplace practice. It also considers how perception, dexterity and legitimacy shape what is possible for different professionals and whether and how they engage. Examples from the implementation of e-health tools in Swedish primary care illustrate how a workplace change can open up participation for some professional groups while constraining it for others. The framework offers a way to analyse for whom opportunities arise, how they are encountered and under what circumstances they are taken up. It may inform future WPL research and analyses of technology implementation in practice.

Members of the public increasingly consult generative artificial intelligence (AI) for health advice, and research has largely asked whether they trust it. Trust is the wrong yardstick. Reliance on health advice is appropriate only when it tracks whether the advice is correct and what an error would cost. We argue for an outcome standard, calibrated reliance, under which four actions (adopt, verify, reject, and escalate to professional care) are judged jointly against advice correctness and the cost of error. Drawing on trust calibration, automation bias, algorithm aversion, advice taking, and heuristic models of credibility, we read a purposive set of human-participant studies against this standard. The studies show both reliance errors. Identical advice is discounted when labeled as AI-generated, which is consistent with underreliance. Low-accuracy AI responses are rated and followed much like physicians' responses, and lay users assisted by large language models choose care dispositions no better than controls, which is consistent with overreliance. Both patterns suggest that lay reliance responds to source and fluency cues more than to correctness. Interventions that require users to act, such as verification affordances, cognitive forcing, and expressed uncertainty, show more promise than passive labels, but no study has yet manipulated correctness and graded clinical risk together while observing verification and escalation. We state five propositions with their evidential status, operational definitions, and a factorial design that would test them.

Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.

Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.

Agentic AI (AAI) systems are a step beyond decision-support AI, where AI acts as an agent in an autonomous way for multiple steps. There are two related organizational problems: the conditions for organizational readiness for adoption, and the governance of delegated decision authority once autonomous AI agents are deployed. Based on a mixed methods Design Science Research (DSR) study, this paper reports on semi-structured interviews with four senior practitioners in the field of AI from regulated European industries as well as a quantitative survey of 302 practitioners. The findings from the empirical analysis show four organizational capability configurations related to AAI adoption: an organizational governance configuration, a graduated delegation logic, a structural governance capacity pattern, and a financial-experimentation tension. Based on the above findings, the study proposes a prescriptive artifact for readiness assessment based on Agentic AI - Agentic AI Readiness and Integration Framework (AAIRF), which consists of five dimensions: organizational capabilities, technological readiness, human factors, institutional context, and agentic dimensions. It then proposes the Agentic AI Delegation Governance Model (AADGM) to operationalize the governance of the authority shift from AI-assisted to AI-autonomous decision making, by defining task characteristics for each delegation threshold and governance mechanism. The answer to the question of governance that readiness frameworks leave unanswered is how much and on what basis to give autonomy to organizations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO 2 emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO 2 emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and Pennsylvania–Jersey–Maryland (PJM). Using Meta’s LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours. In PJM, where subregional MOER profiles are largely homogeneous, spatial flexibility achieves only 0.3% emissions reduction while temporal flexibility reduces emissions by up to 17.2% relative to S1. The emissions-training time tradeoff under temporal flexibility is nonlinear: moderate reductions require marginal increases in training time, but near-zero emissions require nearly four times the baseline training duration. These findings provide grid-specific guidance for developers pursuing near-term decarbonization, and highlight opportunities for further improvement through empirical characterization of data migration overhead.

Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

Background We developed a hospital web application that searches 266 destinations and links results to indoor navigation. Its default retrieval tiers run locally; an optional cloud large language model (LLM) tier requires explicit invocation. Synthetic queries were used because default-tier searches are not server-logged. Objective We examined how post hoc review of an LLM-generated benchmark changed the apparent benefit of completed system updates. Methods Version v2 added pronunciation aliases to v1; v3 added colloquial knowledge, pronunciation forms, destination-level score combination, and false-match rules. Two v3 rules were informed by evaluation-query failures. A clinician and a medical administrative coauthor jointly reviewed 563 synthetic queries without blinding, excluding 129 and rewriting 289 under review-defined policies. The final data contained 401 answerable and 33 no-valid-destination queries. Archived versions were compared across sequential review stages and with lexical and embedding implementations. Results Among the same 192 answerable evaluation-query identifiers and final accepted destinations, rewriting increased top-1 accuracy from 43.8% to 62.0% for v1 and from 56.8% to 63.0% for v3. Their difference remained near 13 percentage points through earlier review stages and decreased to 1.0 point at rewriting. The tested multilingual-E5-small implementation achieved higher top-3 accuracy than v3 (87.0% vs. 69.3%; exploratory P < 0.001), with differences in passage scoring, abstention, and evidence display. For v3, candidate returns occurred on 4/11 reviewed no-valid-destination evaluation queries and 11/29 original queries in a retrospective sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Unblinded benchmark editing changed performance estimates for frozen systems within this synthetic corpus. The findings do not establish improved real-user performance, independent generalization, or comparative clinical safety. The version difference is conditional on the review intervention; neither wording distribution was validated against patient input. Review before optimization and independent user evaluation require prospective assessment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Global Digital Compact, adopted by Member States in September 2024 as an annex to the Pact for the Future, sets shared objectives on digital divides, the digital economy, human rights online, data governance and the international governance of artificial intelligence. Whether those commitments matter depends on what happens in cities, where public services, infrastructure and community life meet digital systems. This paper argues that a city-level deployment of sovereign artificial intelligence is a valid and auditable target for the Compact's localisation, provided that democratic agency is written into the protocols that govern the system rather than left outside them. It brings together four bodies of work developed across a single line of inquiry. First, the topology of city-level AI: governance under Permanent Systemic Instability shifts from territorial monopoly to Flow Sovereignty, the maintenance of coherent, low-surprise trajectories across digital, physical and financial systems, organised through active inference, information-geometric policy navigation, sheaf-theoretic consensus and a 72-hour autonomy standard. Second, the Digital Agora, the rights-based counter-model to the Algorithmic Leviathan, which relocates democratic constraints from the political layer to the protocol layer. Third, the primitives that make such constraints enforceable: layered Sybil resistance, quadratic weighting of preference intensity, and the Minimal Anti-Collusion Infrastructure (MACI), which makes votes private, receipt-free and publicly tallied. Fourth, the cryptographic foundations of verification: zk-SNARKs, the per-circuit trusted setup of Groth16, the universal and updatable setup of PLONK, and Kate–Zaverucha–Goldberg polynomial commitments. The paper composes these into a six-layer deployment architecture, maps it to the Compact's five objectives, states five validity criteria a city deployment must meet, and sets out a pilot programme whose outputs are the local evidence the Compact asks for. It also states the limits: residual trust in setups and coordinators, the trade-off between Sybil resistance and inclusion, prover cost at city scale, and the sovereignty trap of new external dependencies. The work is a design specification; its single computation is an analytic illustration and contains no empirical data. KSCCN article prepared in connection with the GDC Localization Townhall, "Localizing the Global Digital Compact: From global frameworks to local implementation" (UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies, 18 November 2026). Companion to "City-Level AI: The Topology of Command and Information Geometry (Volume II)" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22990597) and "The Algorithmic Leviathan" (Volume I, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22990607). documents.abstract: Research impact quantification plays a crucial role in academic assessment. Conventional citation-based metrics have several limitations in fair and comprehensive research evaluation. They often fail to recognize foundational work that receives limited early attention. They may also overlook sustained influence over time, differences across research fields, citation quality reflected by citation contexts and the expertise of citing authors, and variations in author contributions. We incorporate these aspects at the paper level through four factors: originality-oriented downstream influence, long-term influence, field-specific ranking, and citation quality. At the researcher level, we quantify credit according to author order. Based on these, we propose CLOF, a unified metric framework that quantifies the impacts of papers and researchers in an interdependent and iterative manner. To reduce reliance on manually specified weighting schemes, we employ multiple large language model (LLM)-based paper scorers. Their outputs are aggregated using an α-trimmed procedure to generate robust global signals for learning the combination weights. These learned weights further guide the coupled iterative updates of paper and researcher scores via a Double Iterative Power (DIP) method with theoretical convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on academic datasets show that CLOF uncovers influence patterns across papers and researchers that are not captured by existing impact metrics.

Background/Objectives: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease affecting the central nervous system and significantly reducing the quality of life. Early detection of the disease is critical for slowing its progression and developing appropriate treatment plans. In recent years, artificial intelligence and deep learning methods have begun to play a significant role in clinical decision support systems, particularly due to their high accuracy rates in the analysis of Magnetic Resonance (MR) images. Methods: In this study, a hybrid model was developed for the automatic classification of MS. Two different architectures were used for feature extraction in the developed model. These architectures were selected from among the most successful architectures out of 10 different Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures. Six different classifiers were used to classify the feature maps obtained in the proposed model and pre-trained models. The application of the VOTE operation in the final stage of the proposed model improved its performance. Results: The proposed model yielded competitive results compared to similar studies in the literature and the CNN and ViT architectures used in this study. The accuracy rate achieved with the proposed hybrid model was 97.28%. Conclusions: These results indicate that the proposed model has the potential to support computer-aided MS detection and may provide a useful framework for clinical decision support systems.

Understanding human cognitive processes for reasoning is a key step towards developing human-level AI reasoning systems. Syllogistic reasoning — a classical form of deductive reasoning — is a well-established paradigm for investigating human reasoning, known to elicit systematic cognitive biases such as belief bias and atmosphere effects. In this study, we compare the reasoning patterns of humans and three state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs), namely GPT-4, GPT-4o and o4-mini, across multiple syllogism types with belief andatmosphere effects. Using an online questionnaire, we examine the biases in human syllogistic reasoning and compare this with the LLMs responses. We identify biases and differences in accuracy between different LLMs and humans. Belief-inconsistent statements, which contradict generally accepted common knowledge, and the atmosphere effect impact human and LLM answers. Our results show that, although LLMs outperform human participants, they exhibit human-like cognitive effects. We further evaluate the new reasoning model o4-mini, which performs nearly perfectly on the syllogism reasoning tasks and compare logic, human reasoning and LLM reasoning.

Remote ship operation involves analysing information from various perspectives. However, a standardized educational approach for training remote ship operators is lacking. This study addresses the challenges posed by the cognitive attributes of individuals using remote ship operation and monitoring systems by investigating how different perspectives (first-vs. third-person) impact skill acquisition in ship operation. It introduces the ‘cognitive approach limit circle’ (CLC) concept, a decision-making criterion in ship operation, and formulate two hypotheses. The study conducted repeated ship operation trials from both perspectives in congested traffic scenarios over 100 iterations, analysing the learning trajectory regarding safety and efficiency. Accordingly, mitigating safety and efficiency inclination differences between perspectives is challenging. However, repeated exposure to ship operation experiences facilitates the acquisition of safety and efficiency skills that align with the cognitive attributes of the information utilized. Therefore, in training remote ship operators, initial emphasis on collision avoidance through exercises based on qualitative perceptual data—such as object orientation changes and distance perceived directly through retinal image alterations—rather than quantitative computer-generated information promotes the development of CLC awareness tailored to individual capabilities.

How people imagine the future of artificial intelligence (AI) can play a significant role in shaping the development and use of AI. This study investigates collective future thinking about AI in emerging adults and factors that may influence the valence of the imagined events. Participants (N = 158) were asked to imagine, within 1 minute, as many worrying or exciting events about AI as they could that might happen in the near or distant futures. They also completed measures for their attitudes toward AI, technological readiness, and political ideology. Results showed that participants generated more worrying than exciting events for both near and distant futures. The worrying events primarily concerned ethical issues, unemployment, negative cognitive consequences of reliance on AI, and threats to humankind. Exciting events primarily involved scientific breakthroughs, increased efficiency, and assistance with learning, cognition, and well-being. Moreover, the more positive participants felt about AI and general technology, the more exciting relative to worrying events they imagined. Also, participants who self-identified as more conservative imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who self-identified as more liberal, and women imagined more worrying events than men. These original findings provide insights into the anticipatory process regarding AI and have societal implications for AI development and use.

documents.abstract: This study investigates whether LLM-based Conversational Agents (LLMCAs) could be employed as assistive technologies, helping anyone navigate a website by explaining its content and interactive features, and suggesting actions to accomplish specific goals. This would make the web more accessible especially to seniors, blind users and people with mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the study examines whether such tools can analyze the source code of a webpage to identify its structure and interactive elements, understand which interactive components are required to support users in achieving their goals, and act effectively as assistive technologies. In addition, the work compares leading tools to assess differences in their effectiveness and behavior in supporting accessible web interaction. The work presents two empirical studies in which four popular LLMCA tools are evaluated on a set of public websites, in order to assess their ability to understand web page structures and interactive components and assist users in their tasks. The evaluation combines qualitative and quantitative measures, focusing on accuracy, completeness, and practical usefulness of the responses.Results show a good degree of pertinent and good-quality answers, even on websites with a poorly accessible structure. The user-friendly way to interact with a LLMCA makes it much comfortable to use for the average user. However, the study also highlights that some LLMCAs appear more 'skilled' in accessibility tasks than others. LLMCAs show promising potential not only to complement existing assistive technologies but also to support or replace the human assistance that is often required for many users to effectively access the web.

documents.abstract: Background Patients and caregivers increasingly rely on LLMs for health information, yet their performance in TT, a time-critical urological emergency, remains insufficiently characterized. This study compared three LLMs across content safety, quality, reliability, readability, understandability, and actionability. Methods Twenty-five standardized patient-centered questions were developed based on clinical guidelines, expert consensus documents, and information needs identified through Google Trends. Each question was submitted to GPT-5.6 Sol (High reasoning mode), DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Doubao 2.0 Expert Model, yielding 75 responses. Quality and reliability were assessed using GQS, mDISCERN, and QAMAI; understandability and actionability were evaluated using PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A, respectively. Readability was assessed using six English-language indices, and content deficiencies were also evaluated. Results GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) achieved significantly higher GQS, mDISCERN, and QAMAI scores than the other two models (all overall P < 0.001). Hallucinations and factual inaccuracies occurred in 28.0% and 17.3% of responses, respectively. No hallucinations were detected in GPT-5.6 Sol responses, compared with 44.0% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro and 40.0% for Doubao 2.0 Expert Model. Understandability did not differ significantly among models ( P = 0.0735), whereas actionability did ( P < 0.001), with GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) performing best. All six readability indices differed significantly among models (all P < 0.001). DeepSeek-V4-Pro showed the most favorable relative readability, GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) intermediate performance, and Doubao 2.0 Expert Model the greatest reading difficulty. Conclusions The three LLMs exhibited distinct performance profiles in generating TT-related health information. GPT-5.6 Sol (High reasoning mode) achieved the highest scores for quality, reliability, and actionability, whereas DeepSeek-V4-Pro showed comparatively better readability. Understandability did not differ significantly among models. However, hallucinations, factual inaccuracies, and substantial reading demands remain concerns. These findings reflect model performance under the specific evaluation conditions and at the time of data collection, rather than established clinical effectiveness or safety. GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) may be the most suitable supplementary information tool among the models evaluated, but it should not replace professional medical assessment or clinical decision-making.

documents.abstract: Attentional distraction is an established strategy for reducing acute pain, yet relatively few studies have examined the psychophysiological correlates of gamified biofeedback interventions. This pilot study investigated whether gamified biofeedback tasks can modulate subjective and physiological responses to acute pain. Twenty healthy adults participated in a within-subject experiment consisting of three successive pain conditions, induced by the Cold Pressor Test. The first trial used no intervention, followed by two gamified intervention conditions, presented in a counterbalanced order across participants. One used electrodermal activity (EDA) biofeedback with the Calm The Waves (CTW) system; the other used a visual search task designed to induce cognitive load. Seven participants had prior training in the CTW task (experts). Subjective pain intensity was assessed using a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), and EDA was continuously recorded throughout each two-minute trial. Mixed-design repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted to examine the effects of condition and prior CTW training. Subjective pain ratings differed significantly across pain conditions, F (2, 36) = 11.41, p < .001, ηp² = .388. Pain baseline M = 6.80 (1.10), pain with CTW M = 6.30 (1.90) and pain with Visual Task M = 5.40 (1.70). In contrast, mean EDA did not differ significantly across conditions, nor across participants’ expertise status. These findings suggest that gamified interventions are associated with reduced subjective pain during acute pain exposure, while corresponding changes in average electrodermal activity were not evident. Both real-time physiological biofeedback and sustained cognitive engagement may contribute to acute pain modulation, although further research is needed to determine whether these effects translate into broader self-regulation skills. Future studies with larger samples and clinical populations should investigate whether dynamic EDA measures are more sensitive indicators of physiological changes associated with acute pain. These findings may contribute to the refinement of biofeedback training approaches for acute pain modulation.

Diagnosing root fractures, especially vertical root fractures (VRFs), is one of the most difficult diagnostic issues in endodontics. Despite the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in radiograph interpretation, no pooled diagnostic-accuracy estimates have existed for this question. The aim was to systematically review and meta-analyze the diagnostic accuracy of AI for detecting root fractures across cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), periapical, and panoramic radiography. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore were searched from the date of inception to June 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251121564). Eligible studies used AI to diagnose root fracture with extractable 2×2 diagnostic data. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were derived using a bivariate random-effects model with the hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) modeling. Thirteen studies (2013-2026) were synthesized qualitatively; three (576 fractured, 576 non-fractured teeth) contributed to the meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.90-0.97), and pooled specificity was 0.97 (95% CI: 0.77-1.00). Heterogeneity was substantial for sensitivity (I²=77.9%) and specificity (I²=95.6%), driven largely by one outlying study. The summary point approximated the ideal upper-left corner of SROC space. Certainty of evidence was moderate. AI demonstrated excellent pooled diagnostic accuracy for root-fracture detection, with CBCT-based deep learning models performing best. However, substantial heterogeneity and risk-of-bias concerns temper confidence, pending larger, prospective, externally validated studies.

documents.abstract: Rebound tonometry is widely used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in cats; however, differences in clinical tonometer measurement configuration may contribute to variability in recorded values. This prospective repeated-measures study compared IOP measurements obtained using horizontal and vertical Tonovet Plus clinical measurement configurations in 32 client-owned, systemically and ophthalmologically normal conscious cats. Intraocular pressure was measured in the right eye while the probe was directed toward the center of the cornea and positioned 4-8 mm from the corneal surface. The order of horizontal and vertical configurations was randomized for each cat. Measurements were obtained by one experienced veterinary ophthalmologist and a trained student operator group. In the primary linear mixed-effects analysis accounting for repeated measurements within cats, horizontal configuration was associated with an estimated 2.41-mmHg higher IOP than vertical configuration (β = 2.41 mmHg; 95% CI, 1.39-3.44; p < 0.001). The configuration-associated difference was also observed separately for the experienced instructor (mean difference, 2.81 mmHg; 95% CI, 1.91-3.71; p < 0.001) and across the trained student operator group (2.00 mmHg; 95% CI, 0.81-3.19; p = 0.002). These findings indicate that horizontal and vertical Tonovet Plus clinical measurement configurations may yield different IOP values in conscious cats. As configuration changes may affect instrument handling, restraint, head positioning, and animal responses, the difference cannot be attributed solely to tonometer orientation or mechanics. Consistent configuration is therefore recommended when comparing serial IOP measurements in cats. Further controlled studies are needed to distinguish mechanical, ergonomic, and other examination-related mechanisms.

The rapid advancement of AI-assisted software engineering has brought transformative potential to the field of software engineering, but existing tools and paradigms remain limited by cognitive overload, inefficient tool integration, and the narrow capabilities of AI copilots. In response, we propose Compiler.next , a novel search-based compiler designed to enable the seamless evolution of AI-native software systems as part of the emerging Software Engineering 3.0 era. Unlike traditional static compilers, Compiler.next takes human-written intents and automatically generates working software by searching for an optimal solution. This process involves dynamic optimization of cognitive architectures and their constituents (e.g., prompts, foundation model configurations, and system parameters) while finding the optimal tradeoff between several objectives, such as accuracy, cost, and latency. This article outlines the architecture of Compiler.next and positions it as a cornerstone in democratizing software development by lowering the technical barrier for non-experts, enabling scalable, adaptable, and reliable AI-powered software. We present a roadmap to address the core challenges in intent compilation, including developing quality programming constructs, effective search heuristics, reproducibility, and interoperability between compilers. Our vision lays the groundwork for fully automated, search-driven software development, fostering faster innovation and more efficient AI-driven systems.

Abstract Across living organisms, eusocial superorganisms, human social networks, imperial bureaucracies, financial clearing systems, frontier artificial intelligence architectures, and technological civilizations on cosmic timescales, complex systems exhibit an invariant structural failure signature: they rarely collapse when visibly depleted, instead stalling, oscillating, and fracturing at apparent peak scale. This monograph formalizes Complexity and Information Compression Dynamics (CICD) as a substrate-invariant theoretical framework governing the joint evolution of structural coordination overhead and cross-boundary information compression. Every bounded system operates on a finite flux of gross capacity (E_gross) partitioned between internal maintenance and coordination overhead (E_maint) and net discretionary surplus (E_net). Because relational interdependencies scale super-linearly with effective structural dimensionality (C), every non-modular topology encounters a hard thermodynamic ceiling—the Complexity Maximum (C_max)—where internal upkeep consumes total capacity (E_net → 0). Simultaneously, transmitting high-dimensional internal states across finite-bandwidth internal or external interfaces (B_int) requires lossy compression, elevating the dimensionless Information Compression Friction Index (Φ ≥ 1) above the Landauer–Shannon thermodynamic floor and inflicting structural fidelity loss (ΔΨ). By the Two-Way Coupling Lemma (C ↔ Φ), rising complexity degrades cross-boundary legibility past a Legibility Horizon, while compression reconciliation overhead consumes discretionary surplus and contracts the effective Complexity Maximum downward. When complexity saturation (σ = C / C_max) converges with lossy compression lag, systemic damping vanishes at a critical Hopf bifurcation threshold (σ_crit), inducing Pre-Collapse Oscillatory Judder, pre-critical shock amplification (Λ(σ)), post-critical exponential runaway, and structural epistemic blindness—forcing either a deliberate topological phase-jump behind low-entropy symbolic interfaces or violent involuntary complexity shedding. From these four foundational axioms, the monograph derives four formal corollaries spanning the complete physical phase diagram of bounded scaling—Thermodynamic Fitness Traps, Low-Entropy Interface Kill Switches, Conjugate Compression–Compute Conservation, and the High-Latency Monolith Prohibition—and validates the framework across thirty orders of magnitude in scale. These derivations resolve apparent anomalies ranging from the two-billion-year prokaryotic plateau, eusocial ant-mill cascades, crocodilian ectothermic stasis and somatic-repair energetics, beaver externalized compute loops, sleep as an offline Regime 2 reset, human qualia as a 20-watt executive compression codec, and Homo sapiens as the sole surviving hominin species, to pre-modern imperial fragmentation, the July 1914 European mobilization cascade, the ~4 GHz multi-core microprocessor frequency wall, post-transformer artificial intelligence architectures, and the Fermi Paradox, concluding with a zero-free-parameter empirical falsification protocol. · Authorial & Computational Disclosure: The theoretical framework, core axioms, cross-scale synthesis, and structural direction of this monograph were conceived, directed, and validated by the author. Large language model computational assistance was used to aid in drafting the prose, formalize the mathematical derivations, and perform structural verification under the author's continuous instruction and editorial control.

Digital Twin technologies in maritime applications have primarily focused on individual subsystems, such as vessel machinery, navigation, or environmental monitoring, while limited attention has been given to the integrated representation of human operators, vessel dynamics, machinery, and environmental conditions. To address this challenge, a conceptual Virtual Symbiotic Environment for Maritime Operations (VSEMO) is proposed; the VSEMO integrates human, traffic, docking, environmental, and machinery Digital Twins within a closed-loop system engineering framework. The proposed architecture incorporates Explainable Artificial Intelligence to support transparent operational risk assessment and decision support, while immersive virtual reality provides a realistic environment for adaptive operator training. As an initial proof of concept, a Graph Convolutional Network is developed using synthetic graph-based operational scenarios to demonstrate the feasibility of jointly estimating subsystem-level and aggregate operational risk indicators. Although the computational implementation is limited to snapshot-based synthetic data, the proposed framework establishes a scalable and modular foundation for future real-time Digital Twin ecosystems that integrate physiological sensing, vessel telemetry, environmental information, and explainable artificial intelligence for maritime training and decision support.

The banana agro-export sector in Ecuador constitutes a decisive economic pillar, largely sustained by family farming and small-scale production. However, operational conditions in packing plants expose workers to multiple physical, biomechanical, and chemical hazards. This study analyzes the perception and level of occupational risk across the 8 activities of the packing process using the Dimensional Perceived Risk Assessment tool (EDRP-T), adapted from Technical Prevention Note (NTP) 578. A census population of N = 64 workers distributed across the operational stations was evaluated by applying 10 standardized criteria on a Likert scale (1–5). The results reveal a marked heterogeneity in the risk profile (Kruskal-Wallis H = 28.45, p < .001 for Severity). The De-handing and Selection (M = 3.80) and Bunch Reception (M = 3.70) activities recorded the highest levels of biomechanical risk and lacerations, whereas Fungicide Treatment and Immersion exhibited the highest perceived severity (C1 = 5.0) combined with the lowest personal control (C4 = 2.0). It is concluded that there is a normalization of musculoskeletal disorders and a critical dependence on institutional control measures regarding chemical hazards, leading to recommendations for ergonomic engineering interventions and technological substitution.

The current development of artificial intelligence (AI) is sustained by powerful imaginaries that describe possible technological futures aligning with the normative preferences of influential actors. We show how an AI imaginary driven by “Big Tech” corporate interests and technosolutionism has influenced the development of an AI/cybersecurity imaginary in the UK. Building on the Science and Technology Studies concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, we adopt atechnopolitical lens to examine how external notions of AI progress and development interacted with internal U.K. government commitments to cybersecurity. Drawing on U.K. government texts and interviews with 37 officials, nongovernment experts, and industry actors, we trace the emergence of an AI/cybersecurity imaginary between 2022 and 2024, how intragovernment controversies were negotiated and resolved, and how this imaginary stabilised in U.K. security politics with identifiable outcomes in cybersecurity governance. The article contributes empirical support for the importance of sociotechnical imaginaries in understanding security trajectories, how corporate and technosolutionist imaginaries influence government policy and practice, and offer theoretical insights into the dynamics of imaginary formation and function. AI imaginaries promote the goals and values of science and technology, while technopolitics dominated by corporate actors and technoscientific optimism constrain governmental and social capacity to create and enact alternative imaginaries of future cybersecurity.

Cleft lip and palate (CL/P) are congenital craniofacial conditions that require coordinated, multidisciplinary care from infancy through growth. Presurgical orthopedic and prosthetic appliances, such as feeding/palatal plates and nasoalveolar molding (NAM) devices, are used in selected patients, and digital workflows based on intraoral or three-dimensional (3D) scanning, computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), and 3D printing are increasingly proposed as alternatives to conventional fabrication. This study was conducted to map the available evidence on conventionally and digitally fabricated prosthetic and presurgical appliances for infants and young children with CL/P, to describe the characteristics of that evidence, and to identify research gaps. A scoping review was conducted and reported according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), using a Population–Concept–Context framework. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar were searched. Two reviewers screened records independently. Data were charted using a predefined set of items and summarized descriptively (counts and percentages) and narratively. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was undertaken. Thirty sources were included: 7 systematic reviews (3 with meta-analysis), 1 randomized controlled trial, 2 observational clinical studies, 13 case reports, case series, or technical reports, 4 workflow-development or technical-validation studies, 2 in vitro studies, and 1 narrative review. Twenty-three sources (76.7%) were published in 2021 or later. By focus, 10 addressed feeding/palatal plates and obturators, 4 digital impression or scanning, 5 conventional NAM, 9 digital NAM or presurgical plate workflows, and 2 artificial intelligence (AI)-supported planning. Digital workflows were feasible in all categories and offered advantages in data storage, reproducibility, and virtual adjustment. Improved fit was demonstrated mainly in vitro. The only randomized trial in neonates (n = 30) favored digital over tray impressions, whereas a meta-analysis of five randomized trials found no significant differences between digital and conventional NAM in several presurgical outcomes, with low-to-moderate certainty of evidence. Digital workflows redistributed rather than uniformly reduced work time. Digital technology should be regarded as an extension of established clinical practice rather than an automatic substitute for conventional methods. The evidence base is recent, small, and dominated by low-level designs. Future progress depends on standardized digital protocols, larger randomized trials, long-term follow-up, validated materials, and careful integration of AI with clinical expertise.

The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.

Synthetic experiments compare geometric observations with energy, periodogram and known-reference distance baselines. They illustrate configuration-dependent blind spots and complementary sensitivities. They do not establish general superiority or operational cybersecurity performance. The proposed evaluation protocol prepares comparisons on held-out, labelled incident data at a predefined false-alert budget. No evaluation on real incidents or operational AI-agent traces is included. The archive contains Python scripts, English and French technical notes, a reproduction command, execution records, environment information and SHA-256 checksums. Exact computations, mathematical statements, floating-point diagnostics and synthetic simulations are distinguished. RK-A and RK-B are published separately and referenced as related mathematical work. DESCRIPTION SCIENTIFIQUE — FRANÇAIS COS45 — Observateurs complémentaires de sous-espaces de Hankel : calculs exacts de noyaux, essais synthétiques et protocole d’évaluation Ce dépôt fournit des scripts Python, des notes techniques bilingues, des calculs exacts, des expériences synthétiques et un protocole proposé pour évaluer des observateurs complémentaires de sous-espaces de Hankel. Pour une référence harmonique de onze mesures, les calculs rationnels caractérisent les directions invisibles au premier ordre des observations gauches seules et bilatérales, pour les configurations de Hankel 4 × 8 et 5 × 7. Le noyau commun est de dimension cinq lorsque seuls les projecteurs gauches sont observés. L’observation conjointe des projecteurs gauches et droits le réduit aux deux directions harmoniques. Des minorants rationnels certifiés quantifient la sensibilité hors du noyau commun, avec des conventions de norme explicites. Les expériences synthétiques comparent les observations géométriques à des références fondées sur l’énergie, le périodogramme et la distance à un signal connu. Elles illustrent des angles morts dépendant de la configuration et des sensibilités complémentaires. Elles n’établissent ni supériorité générale ni performance opérationnelle en cybersécurité. Le protocole proposé prépare des comparaisons sur des incidents étiquetés réservés au test, avec un budget de fausses alertes défini à l’avance. Aucune évaluation sur incidents réels ou traces opérationnelles d’agents d’IA n’est incluse. L’archive contient les scripts Python, les notes techniques française et anglaise, une commande de reproduction, les journaux, les informations d’environnement et les empreintes SHA-256. Calculs exacts, énoncés mathématiques, diagnostics flottants et simulations synthétiques sont distingués. RK-A et RK-B sont publiés séparément et référencés comme travaux mathématiques connexes.
